## A Portfolio Approach — Draft for Discussion, Not for Ratification

## 1. What the Two Failed Increases Were Actually Telling Us

| Question | Output required |

The last point deserves emphasis. Three delisted products are not purely a loss; they are an experiment someone else ran on our behalf. | Lever | Gross GM points | Timing |

| Mix management (portfolio, channel, customer, tail cull) | +0.6 to 1.0 | Q1–Q5 |
| Trade promotion redesign (efficiency, not withdrawal) | +1.0 to 1.4 | Q2–Q4 |
| Cost engineering (formulation, packaging, network, complexity) | +1.2 to 1.8 | Q2–Q6 |

Before adding a third move, it may be worth sitting with what the first two produced. ### A note on how this plan was built and how it should be carried

The two previous increases were, I think, technically defensible and organisationally lonely. They were built in Finance, handed to Sales, and presented to buyers as a fact. This plan is built differently: the numbers below are a committed base case, but the sequence deliberately puts alignment *before* announcement — internally across Commercial, Supply, R&D, Finance and Legal, and externally with our customers, so that no buyer is asked to absorb a surprise in a public meeting. Where I have committed to a figure, I have stated the assumption underneath it. Where a figure is a benchmark prior rather than our own data, it is labelled as such.

The central principle for the customer-facing work: **we do not decline, and we do not issue. We re-shape.** Every ask arrives with two or three alternative shapes of equivalent margin value, so that a buyer who cannot accept our first proposal can still say yes to something without losing face internally. That is how we recover margin without a second delisting.

## 1. Executive Summary

**Diagnosis.** The two rejected increases were not a failure of conviction but a failure of **aggregation**. An average increase applied to a portfolio with heterogeneous elasticity over-prices the elastic tail and under-prices the inelastic core. Our volume loss came from the former; unrealised margin still sits in the latter. Combined list movement of ~11% delivered ~6.2% realised net price and ~7.4% volume decline (−13% in price-sensitive segments) — a near-zero net revenue outcome with negative GM$.

**Committed target (base case).**

| | Today | End Q6 | End Q10 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gross margin % | 32.0% | **34.6%** | **36.3%** |
| Cumulative gross recovery actions (GM points) | — | +6.8 | +9.0 |
| Continuing input inflation absorbed (GM points) | — | −2.5 | −3.8 |
| Internal drags (volume, de-absorption, investment) | — | −1.7 | −1.6 |

**We should say plainly to ourselves and to the Board that full restoration to 38.0% within six quarters is not achievable without unacceptable distribution risk.** Under sustained inflation the six lost points are a moving target: at 2.5% forward COGS inflation, roughly 1.7 GM points per year erodes underneath us. The honest commitment is 34.6% at Q6 and 36.3% at Q10, with continuing inflation fully offset in-year from Q4 onward. A plan promising 38.0% by Q6 would be a plan that loses a second retailer.

**Five moves, no single one load-bearing.** Tiered list pricing replacing across-the-board increases; a channel-differentiated pack ladder including a genuine entry price point; mix and tail management we initiate before our customers do; promotion reallocation rather than withdrawal; and cost engineering launched *before* the next price conversation, so we arrive having already shared the burden.

**The negotiation is the plan.** Section 11 is the longest section for a reason. A technically perfect price architecture presented badly to a 17%-of-revenue customer is worth less than a modest architecture presented as a joint category solution.
